source.title_on_document: Harnessing generative AI for collaborative creativity: A study of university students’ engagement and innovation

supplement.where: No supplement or online appendix is identified in the document; the PDF ends with References (PDF pp. 11–13).

paper_design_summary: Fifty undergraduate English majors in a Communication Skills course were randomly divided into AI-supported and no-AI groups of 25 (PDF p. 4, section 3.1). Students collaboratively generated alternative uses for a cardboard box, with ChatGPT-3 available in the AI condition (PDF p. 4, sections 3.2.1–3.2.2). Trained raters scored fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration; post-task student reflections were analyzed separately for perceptions of group dynamics (PDF pp. 4–5, sections 3.2.2.1–3.2.4).

studies.label: Collaborative cardboard-box Alternative Uses Task in a Communication Skills course

assignment.what_was_assigned: Students were randomly divided into AI-supported and no-AI groups. Recruitment from the course was purposive, but allocation to AI assistance was explicitly random (PDF p. 4, section 3.1).
assignment.quote: The students were then randomly divided into two groups of 25: one group performed the task without AI assistance (control group), while the other used AI (experimental group).

arms.name: AI-supported (ChatGPT-3)
arms.description: Received ChatGPT-3 training and used the tool during the same collaborative AUT; students prompted it to develop and advance concepts and were instructed to distinguish AI-generated from human-written material (PDF p. 4, section 3.2.2). Assignment count: PDF p. 4, section 3.1; analyzed count: PDF p. 5, section 4.1.

arms.name: Non-AI control
arms.description: Completed the collaborative AUT without AI, working face-to-face and recording responses on paper or a shared Google document (PDF p. 4, section 3.2.1). Assignment count: PDF p. 4, section 3.1; analyzed count: PDF p. 5, section 4.1.

participants.exclusions: No exclusions or attrition are reported. The paper reports 50 students divided randomly into two groups of 25 (PDF p. 4, section 3.1), and the analysis reports n = 25 in each arm (PDF p. 5, section 4.1).
participants.who: Undergraduate English majors enrolled in the Communication Skills course at the National University of Modern Languages (NUML), Islamabad, in spring 2024; 25 male and 25 female students, ages 18–22, selected purposively from the same course (PDF p. 4, section 3.1).
participants.quote: An independent-samples t-test was used to assess differences in creative output between the two groups: the AI-assisted experimental group (n = 25) and the non-AI control group (n = 25).
participants.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 3287), section 3.1, recruitment, demographics and assignment; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 3288), section 4.1 and Table 1, analyzed arm counts; PDF p. 1, NUML affiliation, Islamabad, Pakistan.

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT-3 (the model label used by the paper; exact deployment/version not specified)
ai_tool.how_used: Students received training before the task, then directed ChatGPT-3 through their own inquiries to generate and develop ideas during collaborative brainstorming. They were instructed to identify AI-generated material separately from human-written material; no fixed prompt protocol or chat logs are supplied (PDF p. 4, section 3.2.2; PDF p. 5, section 4.1).

task.description: Collaboratively generate multiple and varied uses for a cardboard box in the Alternative Uses Task. Responses were recorded on paper or in a shared Google document; the AI arm completed the identical AUT with ChatGPT-3 support (PDF p. 4, sections 3.2.1–3.2.2).
task.duration: 10 minutes of collaborative idea generation (PDF p. 4, section 3.2.1).

outcomes.name: AUT fluency
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of distinct ideas generated, counted from the AUT responses (PDF p. 4, section 3.2.2.3). Two trained raters independently scored the ideas using an adapted rubric; their domain expertise, blinding, score aggregation, and the numeric Cohen’s kappa are not reported (PDF p. 5, section 3.2.2.3). The paper analyzes the two student arms with independent-samples t-tests, n = 25 per arm and t(48), so participant records its reported analysis unit (PDF p. 5, section 4.1 and Table 1). However, the task is described as collaborative group work; how group responses were converted into individual scores is not stated (PDF p. 4, section 3.2.1). Figure 1 repeats the means with standard-deviation error bars (PDF p. 6, printed p. 3289).

eligibility.reason: The paper explicitly states random division of students into AI-assisted and no-AI conditions (PDF p. 4, section 3.1). It analyzes 25 students per arm, meeting the threshold of 50 people exactly (PDF p. 5, section 4.1 and Table 1). Trained raters score the produced AUT ideas on four creativity dimensions (PDF pp. 4–5, section 3.2.2.3; PDF p. 5, Table 1). AI was available during production (PDF p. 4, section 3.2.2; PDF p. 5, section 4.1). The unclear mapping from collaborative group output to participant-level tests is a precision concern that requires clarification before pooling, rather than an absence of any of the three stated eligibility criteria.

one_line_finding: Among 50 analyzed students, the AI-supported arm scored higher than the no-AI arm on fluency (22.8 vs. 15.2), flexibility (11.6 vs. 8.4), originality (7.9 vs. 6.1), and elaboration (24.5 vs. 18.3; PDF p. 5, section 4.1 and Table 1).
open_questions: How were individual creativity scores constructed from the collaborative responses, and were there smaller independent teams or only the described groups of 25? The group procedure and the participant-level independent-samples tests are not reconciled, and no adjustment for collaborative dependence is reported (PDF p. 4, section 3.2.1; PDF p. 5, section 4.1 and Table 1).

What were the full scoring rubric, aggregation rules, originality normative sample, and numerical inter-rater reliability, and were raters blind to condition? These are not supplied despite a statement that Cohen’s kappa was calculated (PDF pp. 4–5, section 3.2.2.3).

What is the denominator for the reflection percentages? Figure 2 and its discussion describe fifty students who implemented ChatGPT-3, while the methods and quantitative analysis assign only 25 students to AI support (PDF p. 7, Figure 2 and accompanying text; PDF p. 4, section 3.1; PDF p. 5, section 4.1).
Which exact model and deployment does the paper mean by ChatGPT-3? The experimental description does not identify a more precise version (PDF p. 4, section 3.2.2).
notes: All markdown lines and all PDF pages were read, including References; there is no appendix in the saved PDF. Field_rct is the screening classification for the university-course setting described in section 3.1, rather than an online panel or a reported laboratory setting (PDF p. 4). Table 1 and Figure 1 report the same four scored outcomes and are not separate studies or separate outcome variants (PDF pp. 5–6). Figure 2 reports reduced evaluation apprehension (80%), fixation on AI-generated ideas (45%), and role ambiguity/AI dominance (30%); these are themes in subjective reflections, not scores on creative outputs, so they are not outcome entries (PDF p. 7, Figure 2; PDF pp. 7–8, sections 4.7–4.9). No between-person diversity measure or unassisted creative follow-up is reported. All four scored outcomes concern work produced with AI available in the treatment arm; post-task reflections do not establish an after_ai performance outcome. No primary outcome designation, preregistration, public data/code link, or reuse of another paper’s participants is stated. The negative t-statistics are preserved exactly as printed; direction is treatment_higher because the AI arm has the higher mean on every measure (PDF p. 5, Table 1). No effect sizes or other statistics were calculated.
